limits: Identification rests on one spectrum with no polarization, no temperature series, no reference spectra, and no database access. The literature values above are recalled from memory and were not verified in this session. The identification is therefore tentative.
Coverage is only 60-1100 cm-1. Bands above 1100 cm-1 (e.g. second-order or D/G-type bands) and any Si 520.7 cm-1 line outside this range cannot be checked. No Si line is seen in 500-530 cm-1.

Noise is about 370 counts per point against a background of about 5000-6600 counts. The ~140 cm-1 feature is about 3 sigma and depends on the baseline model; its position is uncertain by a few cm-1, and its FWHM ranges from about 9 to 13.5 cm-1 depending on the model.

The background is non-monotonic (about 6100 at 60-120 cm-1, about 6600 at 200-400 cm-1, about 5100 above 900 cm-1). A quadratic baseline leaves residual structure at 60-120 cm-1, so weak features there cannot be ruled out. A 16-peak full fit was overparameterized: several broad components hit the sigma bound and fit the background hump, and many narrow ones fit noise. Those components are not reported.

No 72 cm-1 band is present (fit amplitude 1354 +/- 1954 counts, not significant). If the material were Bi2Se3, this would be a strong omission, though sample conditions or instrument response could also suppress it.

The 181.4 cm-1 position is measured after the instrument's own calibration. Calibration accuracy was not checked, and no neon or silicon reference line was available to verify it. A systematic offset of several cm-1 would change which candidates fit.
No cosmic-ray spikes were found: the only isolated high point is the 181 cm-1 band, which spans about 9 points and is therefore a real peak.

Single-spectrum identification cannot distinguish a new mode assignment from a shifted known mode. The 181.4 cm-1 mode is also not uniquely matched to any well-known vdW material in the recalled literature.
